title: Leaving New Orleans with Nat Towles' Creole Harmony Kings; stranded in Tulsa
summary: His first band away from home went to Tulsa, where the job collapsed. A man offered a job at Devonport, Oklahoma, where the band played at an open-air pavilion and broadcast on radio.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Herb, what was the first band with which you left New Orleans? Well, that was Nat Toll's Creole Harmony Kings, a group of New Orleans musicians. We had an engagement to go to Tulsa, Oklahoma, play at the Nails Brothers Pavilion, a colored pavilion there. And after we played there a couple of weeks, the job blew up. We found ourselves stranded in Tulsa. First time I ever left home with a band. What year was that? That was around 1923. And after that job blew up, we were sitting around in Tulsa trying to get a job someplace else. So, a man drove up in a Model T Ford. A couple of the boys and myself were sitting in front of the hotel. Didn't know what to do. We didn't want to come back home with failure. So quick inside of two weeks. So we all decided we'd stick around and try to get a job someplace else. So, as luck had it with us, he stopped in front of the hotel and called me to the car and asked me, Did I know where he could find a certain band he was looking for around Tulsa? So I told him, I said, no, I don't know. I said, but you're talking to an orchestra right here. I said, we just came in from New Orleans and playing at the Nails Brothers swimming pool and the job blew up. He said, well, you're just the fellas we want. I said, I have a good job for you in Devonport, Oklahoma. I guess that's about 70 or 80 miles from Tulsa. So he said, could we hit a band? I said, sure. So we lined up all the boys and went in the lobby of the hotel and gave them an audition. And he was crazy about it. He had a real New Orleans jazz band. Correct. Yeah, so he gave us the tickets and everything. And he had a table set for us and fit for a king. And we ate and everything. So we started to wait that night in the open air pavilion. And we played for the luncheon and supper. And then played that night in the open air pavilion. And we lived in Chandler, Oklahoma. This was about nine miles from Devonport where we was working. And we didn't have no car or anything. When we left here, we were told we went on a train. And he bought us an old-time Dodge touring car for us to make the trip from Chandler to Devonport every night. And we were very된 stuff with stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff We doubled on clarinet once in a while, but we used to battle on the sax. We couldn't get the clarinet player we wanted to leave New Orleans. At that time, the fellows looked like they were afraid to travel from home. It would be a tough job trying to get a musician to leave New Orleans.
That must have been one of the first New Orleans bands in that part of the country.

Yeah, it was. So to popularize Mr. Jack Phillips, that's his name, popularize his restaurant, he had us broadcast over Station, let's see what it is, I have it in the book there. Bristol, Oklahoma. I think later they changed it to the Voice of Oklahoma, which moved to Oklahoma City. Well, that was my first time I ever broadcast.
And that must have been one of the first jazz broadcasts in that part of the country.
Yeah, it was really. He stumbled upon a jazz band just right out of the sky.
